The Trait Library

Nature is a parts bin. For a few billion years, living things have been running real tests — under real pressure, with survival as the referee — and the results are walking, swimming, and flying around us. This library collects the cool, unique traits: every animal, everything, everybody with something worth borrowing.

Every entry carries the same four things: the trait, who has it, the evidence for it, and what the suit — or the wider project — could borrow. And every entry is graded in the open: PROVEN MECHANISM, COULD WORK, SPECULATION, or FORCED. Honest negatives print at full size. Nothing here enters the suit spec on this page's authority — these are graded candidates; sheets get filed only on a ruling.

Batch 01 is the giraffe — the animal that started this — checked hard, because the first entry through the door was a claim about its spots that turns out to be half plumbing, half legend. The door stays open after it: the intake shelf at the bottom holds the next candidates, and the “What are we missing?” door takes new ones from anybody.

Batch 01 — The giraffe 9 entries 2 proven mechanisms 5 could work 1 speculation 1 forced

How to read an entry

Each entry answers four questions, in this order: What does the animal actually do? (the trait, in plain words) · How strong is the evidence? (measured in a living animal, measured on the dissecting table, inferred, or just repeated) · What could the suit borrow? (the translation — the wrench this trait might be) · What's the grade? The grade is about the translation, and it prices in the evidence. Where a famous claim doesn't survive checking, the entry prints the negative instead of quietly dropping it.

Proven mechanism

The mechanism is measured in the animal, and it maps directly onto a buildable thing. The strongest grade the library gives.

Could work

A real mechanism and a plausible translation — but nobody has yet demonstrated it as a working suit system.

Speculation

The claim, or the translation, outruns the measurements. Filed, labelled, and not allowed to ride in on a stronger entry's coat-tails.

Forced

The translation is a metaphor wearing a lab coat. The animal science can be perfectly good and the borrowing still be forced — entry 09 is exactly that.

One more label you'll see inside entries: sample size. Giraffe anatomy studies are often built on very few animals — sometimes one. The grades already price that in; the entries say the number out loud so the price stays visible.

Entry 01 — the seed claim, checked hard

Spots as switchable thermal tiles

Could work

Who has it: the giraffe · Where it came from: this whole library started with one question — how do giraffes use their spots for heat dispersion?

The pop version: “Each giraffe spot is a radiator. Blood vessels under the dark patches dump heat, and the giraffe can switch patches on and off to control its temperature.”

The record, sorted into the three layers the pop version stirs together:

Layer 1 — Anatomy: measured, and genuinely remarkable

Each dark patch is supplied by one single central artery (mean ~0.9 mm across) that divides near the patch centre and sends dense, long, parallel spoke-wheel branches (~0.62 mm) out to the patch margin — a textbook angiosome (one artery's private territory), mapped by arterial lead-oxide injection and dissection. Large veins (mean ~1.66 mm) ring each patch in the pale skin, and arteriovenous (A–V) shunts (~0.12 mm) connect the patch arteries to those ring veins — shunts the researchers describe as of a magnitude “never seen before in any species studied.”

The control group is what makes it: the same team injected a zebra, an African wild dog, and a spotted jaguar. None of them had vascular territories matching their markings, and none had significant A–V filling. On current evidence, the patch-plumbing match is giraffe-only. Under the microscope, patch skin differs too: vessel walls are thinner under patches, vessels sit in two layers beneath them, and sweat glands are significantly larger under patches than elsewhere.

Sample-size label, printed as promised: the injection mapping rests on one dissected giraffe (Taylor et al., 2023, reanalysing G. Ian Taylor's injection studies). And one honest dispute: a separate full-skin histology study describes giraffe sweat glands as inactive (Sathar et al. 2010, via Dagg 2014). Gland size is measured; gland activity is disputed between the two literatures. Both printed; not resolved here.

Layer 2 — Measured in living giraffes: real, with one big confound

Surface temperature: dark patch skin and pale skin show dramatic surface-temperature differences, and infrared thermography of zoo giraffes confirms patches read warmer than the pale skin between them in hot conditions. The confound, at full size: dark fur absorbs more sunlight than pale fur, so a warmer patch in a thermal photo is exactly what plain solar heating predicts even with no blood-flow effect at all. A warm patch is consistent with heat-dumping; it does not demonstrate it.

The strongest functional evidence — survival: in 810 wild Masai giraffes followed photographically for 8 years in Tarangire, Tanzania, spot size interacted with temperature anomalies exactly as the thermal-window idea predicts. Calves and adult males with larger spots survived better in anomalously cold seasons (constrict the patch vessels, keep the heat); those with smaller spots survived better in anomalously hot seasons (less dark, heat-absorbing area wins). Effects were weaker in adult females (Mouchet et al., 2026). That is viability selection measured in the wild — but it is a correlation between spot size, weather, and survival, with land-surface temperature standing in for the animals' actual thermal state. It measures that spot size matters to survival in temperature extremes; it does not measure heat moving through a patch.

A separate mechanism, also measured: larger, rounder spots predicted higher survival in calves' first four months (258 calves), attributed by the authors to camouflage in dappled light; spot traits are heritable (Lee, Bond & Cavener et al., 2018). Spots may be doing two jobs at once — which is exactly why single-story pop versions mislead.

Layer 3 — Hypothesis: the part nobody has watched happen

That a living giraffe actively opens and closes those A–V shunts to shunt warm blood into the ring veins and dump patch heat — the “switchable radiator” picture — is an inference from dead-tissue anatomy. No study has measured blood flow through a patch, or heat flux through patch vs. pale skin, in a living giraffe. Taylor et al.'s own conclusion is that the anatomy “supports the thermostatic concept” — supports, not demonstrates.

Meanwhile, the physiological review literature names evaporation — respiratory, via the nasal system — as the main heat-loss route, with behaviour (shade-seeking, body orientation) doing much of the work (Mitchell & Skinner 2004). If patches contribute, their larger sweat glands raise a possibility the pop version never mentions: patches may dump heat partly by sweating through the window, not only by radiating from it. And the pop claim “giraffes can't sweat or pant” is simply wrong on this record — they have sweat glands, enlarged exactly where the thermal story needs them.

Verdict on the seed claim: the plumbing is real, unique, and measured in unusual detail — for a sample of one dissected giraffe. The function is a well-supported hypothesis with one strong correlational field result and one standing confound. The pop version states as demonstrated fact a control behaviour nobody has yet observed in a living animal. It is stronger than a guess and weaker than its reputation.

What the suit borrows

A cooling skin built as many small, independent tiles instead of one big loop: each tile has its own feed line radiating from a centre port (the angiosome layout), a collector ring around each tile, and a shunt valve at each tile edge that can either route hot coolant through the tile's surface (dump heat) or bypass it straight into the collector ring (keep heat). Zoned, valved, fail-local: one punctured tile loses one tile, not the suit's cooling. Honestly noted: variable-conductance heat panels and valved coolant garments already exist in aerospace practice — the giraffe's contribution is the layout (many small independently shunted territories with ring collectors), not the concept of a thermal window. And no sheet should print “the giraffe switches its spots” as settled.

Sources: Taylor et al., Plastic and Reconstructive Surgery (2023) · Mitchell & Skinner, “Giraffe thermoregulation: a review” (2004) · Sathar, Badlangana & Manger (2010), via Dagg, Giraffe (Cambridge, 2014) · Mouchet, Lee, Bond, Cavener et al., Journal of Applied Ecology (2026), DOI 10.1111/1365-2664.70358 · Lee, Bond & Cavener et al., PeerJ (2018) · zoo infrared surface-mapping, e.g. Prawida et al., AIP Conf. Proc. 2634 (2023).

02 · The pressure garment — tight leg and neck skin

Proven mechanism

Who has it: the giraffe · Evidence: measured in living animals — the strongest-evidenced suit system in this batch

What the giraffe does

The skin and fascia of the lower legs are tight and effectively inextensible, holding tissue (interstitial) pressure at a measured mean of ~44 mmHg, where other body regions run ~1–6 mmHg. Leg arteries thicken abruptly below the elbow and knee into resistance arteries, and leg tissue compliance is so low that a small injected volume raises local pressure 5.5× more than in the neck. Together these stop capillaries leaking under arterial pressures that would blow out a human ankle. The neck joins in: whole-skin mapping found a substantially thickened deep dermis on the front and side surfaces of the neck and across the upper trunk, and the authors conclude the neck and trunk skin “may be regarded as being tight.”

NASA's interest is documented, not folklore: Hargens's giraffe-leg work fed directly into astronaut G-suit and lower-body pressure thinking.

What the suit borrows

Don't fight fluid pooling with a pump — pre-pressurise the limb. A snug, low-stretch skin over the legs (and a firm collar zone at the neck) that holds the tissue at a standing squeeze, so posture changes and acceleration don't get to move the wearer's fluids around in the first place.

The human translation already exists in service (G-suits, compression garments); the giraffe refines the spec — where to be tight, how tight, and pairing skin pressure with thick-walled local “resistance” plumbing.

Sources: Hargens et al., transcapillary fluid-balance studies (1987–2006) · Damkjær et al. (2013) · Sathar, Badlangana & Manger (2010).

03 · Drinking without drowning the brain

Proven mechanism

Who has it: the giraffe · Evidence: measured in life, including recordings in awake animals; the credit split between parts is the unsettled part

What the giraffe does

Dropping the head to drink swings the brain through ~5 m of height; raising it again reverses the problem (fainting). The protection is a system, not a single trick: multiple one-way valves in the jugular veins resisting backflow; large, compliant venous storage in the neck that absorbs the surge; arterial walls that constrict as the head rises to push blood brainward; and the rete mirabile, a fine vessel network at the brain's base that buffers flow — real anatomy, disputed share of the credit. Recordings in awake giraffes show pressure near the heart first falling as the head lowers, then rising again during drinking: the system actively managing the swing, measured live, not inferred (Aalkjær and colleagues, 2025).

What the suit borrows

Any suit loop that crosses big height or posture swings (coolant to a raised helmet, fluid lines in a tall rig) borrows the whole stack: one-way check valves on the return line, a compliant surge reservoir sized to swallow the swing volume, and active constriction on the up-leg when the “head” rises.

The lesson is the redundancy — four partial mechanisms layered, none trusted alone.

Sources: Aalkjær and colleagues (2025) · Aalkjær & Wang, cardiovascular review (2021).

04 · The high-pressure pump — a thick wall, not a big heart

Could work

Who has it: the giraffe · Evidence: measured pressures, masses, and wall dimensions, plus a causal gene experiment in mice

What the giraffe does

It runs mean arterial pressure around 200 mmHg — about twice a comparable mammal's — to perfuse a brain 2 m uphill (measured: MAP ~200–224 mmHg; left-ventricular systolic ~234 mmHg). The famous “280/180” is a peak pairing, not the everyday mean — design numbers should use ~200.

The surprise the measurements forced: the heart is not oversized. Mean 2.68 kg across eight weighed hearts, ~0.53% of body mass — the ordinary mammalian proportion. The adaptation is the wall: left ventricle ~2.9–3.6 cm thick, thickening by adding heart-muscle cells as the neck grows. A thick wall normalises wall tension but costs stroke volume — the giraffe pays that trade openly. And the tissues cope genetically: a giraffe variant of the gene FGFRL1 makes edited mice resist hypertension-driven heart and kidney damage (Liu et al., 2021) — pressure tolerance written into connective-tissue signalling, not just plumbing.

What the suit borrows

For the suit's circulation (coolant or power fluid to raised systems): don't spec a bigger pump — spec a thicker-walled, smaller-cavity pressure pump, and budget the trade the giraffe pays: high pressure, modest flow.

Flagged inside the entry The FGFRL1 half — materials and tissues that tolerate chronic overpressure without damage — grades SPECULATION for a suit. It's a research direction, not a borrowable part, and it doesn't get to borrow this entry's grade.

Sources: Aalkjær & Wang (2021) · Smerup et al. (2016) · Østergaard et al., Anatomical Record (2013) · Mitchell & Skinner (2009) · Liu et al., Science Advances (2021).

05 · The hide — armour as a map, not a slab

Could work

Who has it: the giraffe · Evidence: anatomy measured across whole skins; the protective function is inferred, not tested

What the giraffe does

Skin thickness varies hugely by region — measured range ~1.5 mm to ~18.6 mm, approaching 20 mm at the thickest — with a very thick, collagen-dense deep dermis. The thick ground is the upper trunk and rump and the front and sides of the neck. That flank and rump thickness is argued to blunt lion-claw wounds — an inference from wound patterns; nobody has claw-tested it.

Pop claim, corrected: “thickest skin of any land mammal, twice an elephant's” is not supported. Much of the body is far thinner than the maximum. The thickness is a map, not a uniform — and that turns out to be the borrowable part.

What the suit borrows

Armour graded by body zone: thick, stiff collagen-weave panels where strikes land (back, flanks, neck front), thin elastin-rich skin at the joints — where the giraffe itself keeps elastic fibre density high for movement. Flexibility bought only where the animal buys it. Modern cut-resistant weaves already play in this space; the giraffe contributes the zoning map.

Sources: Sathar, Badlangana & Manger (2010) · Strauss & Packer (2012) · histology baseline: Dimond & Montagna (1975). Sample label: one full skin mapped in depth, two more checked.

06 · The tongue — a soft manipulator that works in thorn fields

Could work

Who has it: the giraffe · Evidence: anatomy plus observed behaviour; performance numbers unmeasured; one famous sub-claim unsupported

What the giraffe does

A ~45–50 cm muscular hydrostat — pure muscle, like an octopus arm in miniature — that wraps branches, threads between acacia thorns, and strips leaves in a spiral pull, for up to ~12 hours of feeding a day. Its surface is specialised kit: electron microscopy shows cone-shaped papillae (tiny grip bumps) near the tip, larger cones further back, and broad lentil-shaped papillae on the raised rear section — a graded grip-and-scrape surface. Thick, sticky saliva coats the thorns it swallows.

Printed negatives: the endlessly repeated “antiseptic saliva heals its wounds” has no study behind it — the anatomy papers map the salivary glands; nobody has tested antisepsis or wound healing. Grip force and puncture resistance of the living tongue have likewise never been measured: the thorn-proofing is anatomy plus observed success, not a tested number.

What the suit borrows

A suit manipulator — retrieval finger, sample collector, repair feeler — built as a boneless hydrostat with a graded papillae-textured skin: fine cones at the tip for grip, coarser scraping structures behind. It could work inside spiky, fragile, or contaminated places a rigid tool would tear up. Soft-robotics hydrostat grippers are a real, active field; the giraffe supplies the surface-texture map and the duty cycle — all day, in thorns, no downtime.

Flagged inside the entry The “self-healing antiseptic coating” version grades SPECULATION on its own. That sheet should not be written — see the negative.

Sources: Pérez et al., “Anatomy of the Mouth of the Giraffe” (2012) · Emura, Okumura & Chen (2013), scanning electron microscopy of one tongue · San Diego Zoo Wildlife Alliance (saliva).

07 · The sensor mast — a retina built in zones

Could work

Who has it: the giraffe · Evidence: measured retinal anatomy; behavioural range claims unmeasured

What the giraffe does

The eyes sit ~5 m up on a laterally placed skull, giving a panoramic field — but the borrowable part is inside the eye. The retina is zoned like a sensor layout: a horizontal visual streak (high resolution along the horizon — the predator line), a temporal area boosting frontal resolution, and a structure found in no other ungulate studied — a dorsal arch of alpha ganglion cells that sharpens the lower visual field and feeds motion information used to steer the tongue while feeding and to watch the ground zone. The counts: ~1.39 million retinal ganglion cells, peak density 14,271 cells/mm², resolving power estimated at 25–27 cycles/degree. Colour vision is dichromatic (two cone types) — good, not human-grade.

Honest limit: “a giraffe can spot a lion at 2 km” is behavioural lore, not a measured threshold. Acuity and layout are measured from retinas; range claims are not.

What the suit borrows

Not the height — a suit can't lend its wearer five metres. The zoned sensor layout: a wide low-resolution panorama for the horizon, a high-resolution forward channel, and a dedicated high-acuity downward channel for the ground at the wearer's feet and the work of their own hands and tools — instead of one uniform camera spec everywhere. Sensor budget spent where the animal spends it. The “living surveillance tower” framing beyond that is just a tall camera, and earns nothing extra.

Source: Coimbra et al., Journal of Comparative Neurology (2013) — wholemount retinal topography and stereology.

08 · The quiet channel — humming, and the infrasound claim checked

Speculation

Who has it: the giraffe · Evidence: the hums are measured; infrasound was looked for in the largest dataset and not found; function unknown

What the giraffe does

Giraffes were long filed as near-silent, with a standing assumption — repeated everywhere — that they must therefore talk in infrasound (sound below human hearing) like elephants. The biggest test of that assumption: 947+ hours of recordings across three European zoos found 65 sustained, harmonic hums, all at night, mean fundamental frequency 92 Hz (lowest ~35 Hz) — low, but above the infrasound line. None of the recorded vocalisations in the whole archive fell in the infrasonic range. The authors state plainly that infrasonic communication in giraffes “needs to be considered with caution.” Earlier infrasound reports (conference-era recordings from the early 2000s) were never matched by that archive.

What the hums are for is not established. The contact-keeping idea — stay in touch when nobody can see anybody — is the authors' hypothesis; the study had no night video, so no caller was ever identified and no reply was ever documented.

What the suit borrows

A low-frequency, low-rate team channel for dark, no-visibility conditions — presence pings and caller-identity signatures rather than speech — is a fair borrowing of the hum as documented.

A suit sheet promising “infrasound comms, like the giraffe” would be building on the one part of the story the evidence actively undercuts. That's why this entry sits at SPECULATION despite the hums themselves being real and on tape.

Source: Baotic, Sicks & Stoeger, BMC Research Notes (2015).

09 · Micro-sleep — the rest state that doesn't transfer

Forced

Who has it: the giraffe · Evidence: measured solidly, by two methods — no complaint about the animal science; the borrowing is what's forced

What the giraffe does

It sleeps in fragments: hours of standing doze and inactivity, with true deep (REM) sleep rationed to minutes. Wild accelerometry (movement sensors) measured ~2 deep-sleep events a night totalling ~8.6 minutes — and none at all on roughly 1 in 5 nights. Zoo totals run ~4.6 hours of all sleep, with only ~13 minutes of it paradoxical (REM). It's a predation-driven rationing system: deep sleep needs the vulnerable neck-curl posture, so the animal buys it in minutes, often with herd-mates standing watch.

Why it's filed — at full size

There is no honest suit translation. A human wearer's brain is not negotiable down to nine minutes of REM by suit design — human sleep need doesn't compress like that — and the giraffe itself pays for the ration with a herd-watch system and, on the zoo numbers, far more total rest than the myth suggests. “Suit rest-state inspired by giraffe micro-sleep” would be a scheduling poster, not a mechanism.

Filed anyway, with its grade, because the rule of this library is that honest negatives print at full size — including the ideas that don't make it.

Sources: Frontiers in Mammal Science (2023), wild accelerometry · zoo behavioural study, South African Journal of Wildlife Research.

The grade table — Batch 01 at a glance

This is the sheet queue in one view: what each ability is, how strong the evidence is in the animal, and the grade the translation carries. A grade can be lower than the animal science — entry 09's science is solid and its grade is still FORCED, because the grade judges the borrowing.

#AbilityEvidence in the animalGrade
1Spots as switchable thermal tilesAnatomy proven (unique, measured, n=1 specimen); live switching a hypothesis; survival correlation strong (Mouchet et al. 2026)Could work
2Tight leg/neck skin pressure garmentMeasured in life (44 mmHg tissue pressure; compliance)Proven mechanism
3Head-drop pressure regulation stackMeasured in life, incl. awake recordings (Aalkjær et al. 2025); credit split unsettledProven mechanism
4Thick-walled high-pressure pumpMeasured (MAP ~200 mmHg; wall 2.9–3.6 cm; heart mass normal)Could work
5Graded hide armour mapAnatomy measured (1.5–18.6 mm map); protective function inferredCould work
6Hydrostat tongue manipulatorAnatomy + observed behaviour; force/puncture unmeasured; “antiseptic saliva” unsupportedCould work
7Zoned sensor-mast retinaMeasured retinal topography (Coimbra et al. 2013)Could work
8Low-frequency night channelHums measured (92 Hz); infrasound not found in 947 hours; function unknownSpeculation
9Micro-sleep rest stateMeasured — and non-transferable to a human wearerForced

Standing cautions carried with the queue: the spot-radiator story must keep its labels (anatomy proven, switching unobserved, dark-fur solar confound standing) · “280/180” is a peak pairing — design numbers use the measured mean (~200 mmHg) · the giraffe heart is ordinary-sized; any copy implying a giant heart is wrong on the record · giraffe anatomy sample sizes are small, often n=1 — the grades price that in, and sheet copy must not quietly upgrade them.

The intake shelf — named, not yet checked

The bin is bigger than one animal. These candidates have been named — in conversation, in design notes, in the wild — but the check hasn't run on them yet, so this shelf makes no claims: each line is the claim to be checked, written the way it arrived. When the research runs, a candidate either graduates to a full graded entry above or gets its honest negative printed. Nothing skips the line.

The kingfisher's beak

Awaiting check

Claim to check: a diving bird's beak shape is what quieted the bullet train's tunnel-boom problem — a bird's face, deployed at 300 km/h. If it holds, it's the library's proof that the bin works outside suits too.

Gecko feet

Awaiting check

Claim to check: grip with pure molecular stick — no glue, no residue, reusable indefinitely. What a suit's hands and boots would borrow is obvious; whether the mechanism scales to a human's weight is the question the check has to answer.

The pit viper's infrared organ

Awaiting check

Claim to check: a bolt-on heat sense, separate from the eyes. It's also the standing counter-example in the project's mist work — the sense a mist sheet can't hide from, already shipping in nature as an organ.

The bombardier beetle's reactor

Awaiting check

Claim to check: a pulsed chemical reactor in the abdomen, mixing and firing in controlled bursts without cooking its owner. The same beetle surfaced in the dragon file — the closest chemistry in nature to fire.

The axolotl's regrowth

Awaiting check

Claim to check: an animal that regrows its own heart and parts of its brain. For the suit's self-repair thinking it's a living proof-of-concept — seal first, and something out there may honestly complete the sentence.

Everybody

Open shelf

The library's charter says every animal and everything and everybody with a cool, unique trait. Human traits, plant traits, traits of whole systems — if it ran a real test and passed, it belongs on a shelf. The door below is how it gets here.

The why-chains, run to the bottom

This page's method: ask why until why cannot be asked — then how, and act. Every stated fact carries its why, and the why under that; a chain that stops early is labelled as stopped, never dressed up as the bottom.

Chain 1 — Why does a spot have its own artery?

Why?

Why does each patch get one private artery, spoke-wheel branches, a ring of veins, and shunts between them? → Because on the dissecting table, that's the layout — an angiosome per patch, found in no other spotted animal checked.

Why?

Why would selection keep plumbing that elaborate? → The best field answer: spot size tracks survival through temperature extremes in 810 wild giraffes (Mouchet et al. 2026) — the trait is being selected on, in the direction the thermal story predicts.

Why?

Why does the blood move — is the giraffe really switching patches on and off? → Nobody has measured flow or heat flux through a living patch. The chain stops here, at a labelled gap, with a standing confound beside it (dark fur is warm in the sun either way).

Bedrock not reached — labelled, not dressed up.
How → Act: the engineering borrowing doesn't need the giraffe's reason to be settled. The tile layout is sound either way, so it enters the queue — graded COULD WORK, carrying its labels, until someone measures a living patch and the chain can run one why deeper.

Chain 2 — Why doesn't it faint, leak, or blow a vessel?

Why?

Why is the pressure extreme at all? → The brain sits ~2 m above the heart, and gravity taxes every centimetre of the column; pressure at the brain must stay normal, so pressure at the heart runs ~200 mmHg mean.

Why?

Why don't the legs leak under that? → Thick-walled resistance arteries plus an inextensible skin-and-fascia pressure garment holding tissue at ~44 mmHg.

Why?

Why doesn't drinking flood or starve the brain? → A layered stack — jugular valves, venous storage, arterial constriction, the rete buffer — measured working in awake animals.

Bedrock reached: physics (hydrostatics) plus measured anatomy.
How → Act: build suit loops the way the animal builds its circulation — pressure held by the skin, swings swallowed by layered, redundant mechanisms, no single part trusted alone. This chain is why entries 02 and 03 carry the library's top grade.

Chain 3 — Why a library? Why grade at all?

Why?

Why mine animals for suit parts? → Because nature ran the test runs — billions of years of them, under real pressure, with survival as the referee. An imagined solution is a guess; a living trait is a result.

Why?

Why grade every entry, including a FORCED at full size? → Because an ungraded bin fills up with metaphors wearing lab coats, and a sheet built on a metaphor fails on a person. The grade is what keeps the bin honest.

Bedrock reached: a decision — the house rule that nothing enters the suit spec without a grade and a ruling.
How → Act: file candidates here, in the open, with the evidence priced in. Sheets get drafted from this queue only on a ruling — and the door below keeps the bin growing.

What are we missing?

This library was started by one person pointing at one animal. Somebody out there knows an animal we don't — a trait that ran a test we'd never think to run. If you know one, or you spot a claim here the record doesn't carry, or you can push one of the stopped chains a why deeper, say so: what's missing, what's wrong, and what the tool you really need looks like. Help us make these the tools you really need.

Tell us on the Poster Board →
Public, no account needed. You can also name a whole topic we haven't built anything for yet: “we need something for this.” Those requests become build candidates in the regular flow.
